claim: Every real m-by-n matrix admits real singular value decomposition; the singular values are nonnegative
notes: Real case only; complex requires conjugate transpose

claim: Nonzero singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of A transpose A and corresponding left vectors are Av/sigma
locator: Notes: eigenvectors of A^H A and AA^H
notes: Numerical implementation is not recommended via normal equations

claim: Thin SVD has U shape (m,q), singular-value vector q and Vh shape (q,n), q=min(m,n)
notes: For complex data Vh is conjugate transpose

claim: Every rank-r matrix equals the sum of its r nonzero singular-value dyads
notes: Sign choice and repeated subspaces not unique

claim: Truncated SVD gives an optimal rank-at-most-k approximation in Frobenius and spectral norm
locator: Eckart & Young 1936 abstract; lower-rank matrix approximation
notes: Theorem cited as historical source; modern norm formulation corroborated by Stanford lecture

claim: Proof for a theorem originally stated but not proved in the 1936 work was provided by Johnson in 1963
notes: Attribution avoids implying a proof was in original 1936 paper

claim: Squared Frobenius residual sum equals the squared discarded singular values; spectral residual equals sigma_(k+1)
locator: Low rank approximation and extremal gain
notes: k<r for sigma_(k+1); zero for k=r

claim: The diagonal(9,4,2,1) example has total energy 102 and k=2 retains 97/102
notes: Not source empirical result; rank-k storage k(m+n+1) includes U Sigma V

claim: For centered n-by-d data, right singular vectors diagonalize sample covariance X^T X/(n-1)
locator: SVD and matrix methods; covariance derivation
notes: n>1, centered columns; no scaling by default

claim: SVD gives pseudoinverse by inverting nonzero singular values; tiny singular values amplify noise
notes: Rank-deficient full inverse sensitivity is unbounded

claim: Randomized partial decomposition captures a leading subspace using sampling and then factors compressed matrix
notes: Approximate, not a general exact SVD
